summary: A memory leak is heap memory that is no longer reachable by the program but was never freed. It cannot be reused, so long-running programs slowly consume all available memory.

sections.heading: What a leak is
sections.body: You allocate with `malloc`, lose every pointer to the block (or forget `free`), and the allocator still considers it in use. The block stays reserved until the process exits.

sections.heading: Common causes
bullets: Forgetting `free` on some path, especially early returns and error paths.
Overwriting the only pointer: `p = malloc(...)` twice without freeing the first.
Losing the pointer when it goes out of scope.
Freeing a container but not the elements it owns.

sections.heading: Consequences
bullets: Slowdown from paging and cache pressure.
Out-of-memory failures; the OOM killer may terminate the process.
Worst in servers and daemons that run for weeks.

sections.heading: Prevention
bullets: Pair every allocation with exactly one free in a clear owner.
Use a single cleanup label (`goto cleanup`) so every error path frees resources.
Do not overwrite a pointer before freeing it.
Wrap resources in create/destroy function pairs.

sections.heading: Finding leaks
bullets: Valgrind: `valgrind --leak-check=full ./prog` lists lost blocks with allocation stacks.
AddressSanitizer's LeakSanitizer: `-fsanitize=address` reports leaks at exit.
Static analysis (clang-tidy, cppcheck) flags obvious missing frees.

sections.body: Valgrind distinguishes 'definitely lost' (no pointer remains), 'indirectly lost' (reachable only through a leaked block), 'possibly lost' (only interior pointers remain), and 'still reachable' (pointer exists at exit, often intentional globals).
A leak is forgetting to free; a dangling pointer is using memory after freeing. Over-correcting one tends to cause the other, so ownership rules matter more than reflexes.

Allocate many short-lived objects from one arena and release the whole arena at once. It removes per-object lifetime tracking, eliminates most leaks, and is fast. Compilers and request handlers commonly use it.
The same discipline applies to `fopen`/`fclose`, sockets, and mutexes. Leaking descriptors hits the per-process limit long before RAM runs out.

takeaways: Check every exit path, especially error returns.
Use Valgrind or ASan/LSan in testing.
Consider arenas or clear ownership to simplify cleanup.
